newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa unions threaten fresh strike in 14 days.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa unions threaten fresh strike in 14 days.

text.p: South Africa's largest trade union movement has warned it is ready for a war of nerves over planned new labour laws, threatening a repeat of Monday's one-day strike unless employers changed their stance within 14 days.
The Congress of South African Trade Unions (Cosatu) called the 24-hour action and said two million workers had responded.

South African business, however, said support for the strike had proved limited and many employers had made contingency plans -- employing temporary workers, closing down for the day or granting leave to workers -- which had minimised the impact.
The strike was the third national stoppage since the 1994 elections which brought President Nelson Mandela's government to power.
Unions and witnesses said at least 40,000 strikers marched peacefully through the centre of the industrial capital Johannesburg in the biggest of a series of rallies around the country.
An estimated 151,900 miners, out of a total workforce in the mines of around 500,000, downed tools, according to the National Union of Mineworkers.
Mining houses reported a mixed impact from the action on production of precious metals.
Gold mines reported a varying response to the strike call with some shifts halted completely but many mines still working, although with above-average absenteeism.
The main platinum mines continued to operate, although Anglo American Platinum Corp Ltd said production at its smaller Lebowa Platinum Mines Ltd and Potgietersrust Platinums Ltd mines had been hit.
Toyota South Africa Ltd said its Prospecton plant, employing 5,500 people outside Durban, was shut and it risked losing production of 450 vehicles.
Clothes makers around Cape Town said two-thirds of workers stayed away, and the city's building sector had absenteeism of 80 percent.
The employment bill, approved by cabinet in April, sets a 45 hour working week and four months' maternity leave.
Cosatu, which represents 1.9 million members, wants a 40 hour week phased in within five years, six months' maternity leave and the minimum age for formal employment to be set at 18.

Cosatu General Secretary Sam Shilowa told an afternoon news briefing the federation expected the influential Business South Africa employers' group to come back with revised proposals within 14 days, otherwise there would be a continuation of strike action.
Business South Africa earlier attacked the strike in a country with unemployment at around a third and relatively high labour costs.

Opposition politicians agreed with business. The Zulu-dominated Inkatha Freedom Party said the strike served the interests of "myopic trade unions" and would hurt jobs and worsen inflation, while the former ruling National Party said it would serve to inhibit new investment in South Africa.
